qualifications: Medical diagnosis alone does not establish indication. Use assessed gastrointestinal function,nutrient/fluid adequacy,growth and safe enteral access.
2017 tables mix adult and pediatric advice. No adult bowel-length or fistula-output cutoff used as a pediatric rule.
No numeric catheter dwell-time,peripheral fluid allowance,macronutrient concentration maximum,osmolarity cutoff or fixed PN start/weaning schedule newly adopted.
No universal pediatric PIVrotation rule,adult femoral-site rule,portinfection guarantee or dedicated-lumen benefit adopted.
PeripheralPN evidence limited and individualized. Midline remains noncentral; PN suitability cannot be inferred from device name.

before.question: Which condition is a common pediatric indication for PN when enteral needs cannot be met?
choices: Necrotizing enterocolitis
Uncomplicated seasonal rhinitis
Stable myopia
A healed paper cut
before.rationale: Necrotizing enterocolitis can make enteral feeding unsafe or inadequate.

after.question: Which child has the clearest indication for PN after nutrition and gastrointestinal assessment?
choices: A child with necrotizing enterocolitis whose safe enteral intake cannot meet assessed needs
A child with short bowel syndrome who meets assessed nutrient, growth, and hydration goals through tolerated enteral feeding
A child receiving cancer treatment who tolerates enough oral nutrition to meet assessed needs
A child with kidney disease who meets nutrient needs through oral and enteral intake
after.rationale: PN is indicated when safe oral or enteral delivery cannot meet the child's assessed needs. Necrotizing enterocolitis can create that situation; short bowel syndrome, cancer treatment, or kidney disease alone does not establish a PN indication.

before.question: What is the strongest reason to choose central rather than peripheral access?
choices: The required concentration and duration cannot be delivered safely through peripheral veins
Central access prevents every infection
Peripheral access cannot deliver any fluid
Central access removes metabolic limits
before.rationale: Central blood flow permits more concentrated therapy, but metabolic and catheter risks remain.

after.question: What most strongly supports choosing central rather than peripheral access for pediatric PN?
choices: The required formulation and expected duration cannot be delivered safely through peripheral veins
The peripheral cannula is newly placed, so the full concentrated formulation can be used without review
A midline is available, so peripheral osmolarity limits no longer apply
Central access would allow the prescribed dextrose dose to exceed the child's metabolic tolerance
after.rationale: Choose access that can safely deliver the required formulation for the expected duration. A new peripheral cannula or noncentral midline does not remove osmolarity limits, and central access does not remove metabolic or catheter risks.

choices.review: Midline does not reach central veins and retains peripheral osmolarity limits:Table5.2midline row.

before.question: Which risk remains important with a pediatric PICC?
choices: Infection, thrombosis, malposition, and loss of access
Guaranteed embolism prevention
Elimination of compatibility concerns
Automatic long-term sterility
before.rationale: Central devices require active mechanical, thrombotic, and infection surveillance.

after.question: Which plan best addresses the continuing risks of a pediatric PICC used for PN?
choices: Monitor for infection, thrombosis, malposition, and loss of access while reassessing device need
Monitor for infection but omit thrombosis assessment because the insertion site is peripheral
Confirm the tip only at insertion and disregard possible tip retraction as the child grows
Review nutrient compatibility but omit catheter surveillance while the pump runs normally
after.rationale: A PICC remains a central device with infectious, thrombotic, and mechanical risks. Tip position may need reassessment during growth, and a functioning pump or peripheral insertion site does not establish device safety.

choices.review: Tip may retract during growth and position may need reassessment:Question5E final paragraph.

teaching.heading: Use PN when the gut cannot yet meet the need

before.heading: Use PN when the gut cannot yet meet the need
before.body: Common indications include necrotizing enterocolitis, gastroschisis, intestinal obstruction or dysmotility, short bowel syndrome, severe malabsorption, high-output fistula, prolonged ileus, and treatment-related gastrointestinal injury. PN supports the interval in which safe enteral delivery cannot meet the assessed goal. It does not remove the need to reassess enteral readiness.

after.heading: Use PN when the gut cannot yet meet the need
after.body: Necrotizing enterocolitis, gastroschisis, obstruction, dysmotility, short bowel syndrome, severe malabsorption, high-output fistula, prolonged ileus, and treatment-related intestinal injury can prevent adequate feeding. The diagnosis alone is not the indication: assess whether the gut can be safely accessed and can provide the nutrients and fluids needed for growth. PN may provide all nutrition or supplement tolerated oral or enteral intake. Reassess gastrointestinal function and enteral readiness as the condition changes.

teaching.heading: Match access to concentration and duration

before.heading: Match access to concentration and duration
before.body: Peripheral access limits final concentration and is vulnerable to infiltration and phlebitis. Central access supports concentrated therapy but introduces infection, thrombosis, malposition, and device risks. Umbilical venous catheters can provide early neonatal access when positioned and managed correctly. PICCs, tunneled catheters, and ports are selected according to duration, anatomy, care setting, and the need to preserve access.

after.heading: Match access to concentration and duration
after.body: Peripheral PN is a short-term option when the required nutrients fit within peripheral osmolarity limits and the patient can tolerate the necessary fluid volume. Monitor for infiltration, extravasation, and phlebitis. Central access permits more concentrated formulations but retains infection, thrombosis, malposition, and access-loss risks. Select PICCs, tunneled catheters, or ports according to expected duration, developmental stage, other intravenous therapies, anatomy, care setting, and access preservation. Use the smallest device and fewest lumens that meet the patient's needs, and confirm and document central tip position before PN begins. An appropriately positioned umbilical venous catheter can provide short-term neonatal access.

clauseMap.clauses: Central concentration with infection,thrombosis,malposition and access-loss risks.

before.heading: Account for concentration and osmolarity
before.body: Greater dextrose and amino-acid concentrations raise osmolarity. A classroom estimate can help screen an order, but final peripheral suitability depends on the complete formulation, access, validated policy, and vein tolerance. Central access does not make unlimited carbohydrate delivery metabolically safe.

after.heading: Account for concentration and osmolarity
after.body: Greater dextrose and amino-acid concentrations raise osmolarity. Screen the complete formulation, including electrolytes, for the proposed route; a classroom estimate alone does not establish peripheral suitability. Review the applicable formulation limits, vascular access policy, vein tolerance, and fluid allowance. Dilution may require more fluid than the patient can tolerate or may limit nutrient delivery. Central access can accommodate a concentrated formulation, but it does not remove metabolic limits on carbohydrate delivery.

clauseMap.clauses: Classroom estimate alone cannot establish peripheralsuitability;policy,vein tolerance,fluid allowance matter.
Central accommodatesconcentration but retains carbohydrate metaboliclimits.

summary.text: Pediatric PN starts with developmental age, growth, gastrointestinal function, expected duration, and fluid tolerance. Match the vascular device to the complete formulation and the patient's needs.

concepts.text: Preterm, neonatal, infant, child, and adolescent context

application.text: Document age and developmental context, dosing weight, nutrition deficit, why the enteral route is insufficient, expected duration, access type and tip location, fluid allowance, and the conditions that will trigger reassessment.

keyPoints.text: Age and developmental stage change the prescription.
PN requires both nutrition need and an inadequate gastrointestinal route.
Prompt initiation in preterm infants follows appropriate access.
Access determines what can be delivered safely.
